title: The ML workflow from start to finish
intro: From raw question to working model: the eight steps of an ML project, under- and overfitting shown interactively, and the fit–predict–score trio that sounds the same across all of scikit-learn.

sections.title: The eight steps at a glance

blocks.html: An ML project is not a straight line but a loop: you evaluate, learn, and go back to an earlier step. The order below is the coat rack every project hangs on — from school assignment to production system. The pitfall column is at least as important as the steps themselves.

rows: make the task concrete and measurable (T, E, P)
“we want to do something with AI”
too little data, or biased data
immediately picking the most complex model
accidentally also training on test data
score on test data, pick the right metric

blocks.html: The evaluation in step 7 almost always sends you back: bad score? Then you choose different features (step 4), a different model (step 5) or collect better data (step 2). Experienced data scientists spend most of their time in steps 2 through 4 — not in picking exotic models.

sections.title: Under- and overfitting in one picture

blocks.html: Two ways a model can fail: underfitting — the model is too simple and scores badly on train and test data — and overfitting — the model is too complex, memorises the noise in the training data and surprises you with a bad test score. In between lies the sweet spot: complex enough to capture the pattern, simple enough to generalise.

The chart below plots both errors against model complexity. The training error always goes down (more complex = better able to imitate). The test error follows at first and then rises: that is where overfitting begins. Drag the sliders to see how a more sensitive model (higher “noise sensitivity”) or an earlier “bend” strengthens the U-shape.

blocks.title: Train and test error against model complexity
blocks.subtitle: The U-shape of the test error is the hallmark of overfitting. Drag the sliders — the live metrics track the lowest test error and the gap between train and test error on the right.

rows: more complex model, more or better features

blocks.html: In practice this is the diagnostic tool for step 7 of the workflow: compare train and test score. Small gap = healthy model; large gap = overfitting; both bad = underfitting. Regularisation (chapter 3) is the classic remedy against overfitting.

One of the strengths of scikit-learn: every model has the same three methods. fit(X_train, y_train) trains — the model learns its parameters. predict(X) applies the model to new samples. score(X_test, y_test) judges the quality on unseen data. Whether you choose KNN, LogisticRegression or an SVM: this trio never changes.

blocks.caption: the trio in action
blocks.source:
import numpy as np
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split
from sklearn.linear_model import LinearRegression

X = np.array([[1,  5, 1], [3, 12, 2], [4, 15, 1],
              [7, 23, 3], [9, 30, 2], [2,  9, 1],
              [6, 20, 3], [8, 26, 2]], dtype=float)
y = np.array([18, 12, 10, 6, 4, 15, 8, 5], dtype=float)

X_train, X_test, y_train, y_test = train_test_split(
    X, y, test_size=0.25, random_state=0)

model = LinearRegression()
model.fit(X_train, y_train)                      # 1) learn
print('coefficients   :', model.coef_.round(2))
print('intercept      :', model.intercept_.round(2))
print('predictions    :', model.predict(X_test).round(1))          # 2) apply
print('test score (R2):', model.score(X_test, y_test).round(2))    # 3) judge

blocks.html: The coefficients that fit produces together form the prediction equation — exactly the rules the model learned by itself. What such an equation looks like, which loss function trains it and how you regularise it, is the subject of chapters 1 through 4 of this site.

Checklist before you start coding:

  • Can I formulate my question as a prediction (number or category)?
  • Do I have data that actually contains the answer — and enough rows?
  • Do I know how I will measure success (which metric, which threshold)?
  • Have I split train and test data before anything else?
  • Am I starting with a simple model as a baseline?
Further reading: chapter 1 dives straight into scikit-learn, chapter 2 opens the mathematics, chapters 3 and 4 cover logistic regression and SVMs, and chapter 5 the evaluation metrics.
